content: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) is a serious adverse reaction to certain medications, such as bisphosphonates, denosumab, and antiangiogenic agents, which are commonly used to treat cancer and osteoporosis. This condition involves the progressive destruction of bone in the jaw, either the mandible or maxilla. The likelihood of developing MRONJ depends on the specific drug, its dosage, and the duration of exposure. For example, MRONJ is rare with oral bisphosphonates or denosumab for osteoporosis, but more common with intravenous bisphosphonates used in cancer treatment. MRONJ is associated with significant morbidity, negatively impacts quality of life, and is difficult to treat. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of various interventions compared to no treatment, placebo, or active controls for both the prevention and treatment of MRONJ. For prevention, the primary outcome was the incidence of MRONJ, while secondary outcomes included quality of life, time-to-event, and rates of complications or side effects. For treatment, the primary outcome was the healing of MRONJ, with secondary outcomes including quality of life, recurrence, and rates of complications or side effects. The review included 13 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1668 participants, with eight new studies added since the previous review. The studies were diverse in their interventions, making meta-analysis impossible. The certainty of the evidence for both prevention and treatment of MRONJ was rated as low or very low. Prevention of MRONJ: 1. Dental Examinations and Preventive Treatments: One RCT compared standard care to regular dental examinations every three months combined with preventive measures, such as antibiotics before dental extractions and techniques to close wounds to avoid bone exposure. This study, conducted in men with metastatic prostate cancer treated with zoledronic acid, suggested a reduced risk of MRONJ (RR 0.10, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.39, 253 participants). However, secondary outcomes were not assessed. 2. Dentoalveolar Surgery and Preventive Measures: Five RCTs evaluated various interventions to reduce the risk of MRONJ after dental surgery: Plasma rich in growth factors placed in the extraction site, in addition to standard care, was compared to standard care alone (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.51, 176 participants). Delicate surgical techniques with primary wound closure were compared to non-traumatic tooth extraction with secondary wound closure, with no cases of MRONJ reported in either group. Primary closure of the extraction socket using a mucoperiosteal flap was compared to the application of platelet-rich fibrin without primary closure, with no cases of MRONJ in either group. Subperiosteal wound closure was compared to epiperiosteal wound closure (RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.56, 132 participants). Treatment of MRONJ: 1. Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBO): One RCT evaluated HBO in addition to standard care (antiseptic rinses, antibiotics, and surgery) compared to standard care alone. The results showed no significant difference in healing rates (RR 1.56, 95% CI 0.77 to 3.18, 46 participants). 2. Surgical Techniques: Autofluorescence-guided bone surgery was compared to conventional bone surgery, with no significant difference in healing rates (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.37, 30 participants). Autofluorescence-guided sequestrectomy was compared to tetracycline fluorescence-guided sequestrectomy, with no significant difference at one-year follow-up (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.30, 34 participants). 3. Growth Factors and Platelet Concentrates: Platelet-rich fibrin after bone surgery was compared to surgery alone (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.22, 47 participants). Bone morphogenetic protein-2 combined with platelet-rich fibrin was compared to platelet-rich fibrin alone (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.29, 55 participants). Concentrated growth factor with primary wound closure was compared to primary wound closure alone (RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.81 to 2.34, 28 participants). 4. Pharmacological Interventions: Teriparatide 20 μg daily was compared to placebo in addition to standard care (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.31 to 2.95, 33 participants). Teriparatide 56.5 μg weekly was compared to teriparatide 20 μg daily in addition to standard care (RR 1.60, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.44, 12 participants). Authors' Conclusions: For the prevention of MRONJ, one open-label RCT provided limited evidence that regular dental examinations and preventive treatments may reduce the incidence of MRONJ in individuals receiving intravenous bisphosphonates for advanced cancer. However, the certainty of this evidence was very low. There is insufficient evidence to confirm or refute the effectiveness of other interventions for MRONJ prevention, particularly in patients undergoing dentoalveolar surgery. While some interventions showed potential benefits, the studies were underpowered, and larger trials are needed to confirm these findings. For the treatment of MRONJ, the available evidence is insufficient to confirm or refute the benefit of any specific intervention, in addition to standard care. Further research is required to establish effective treatment strategies for this challenging condition.
